remarks_1999: Inscription on fragment of original backing in Metropolitan Museum of Art file indicates, "Abstraction, IX charcoal"(Stieglitz, First Municipal Art Exhibition label, black ink). Whitney Archive indicates, "Infor. from Miss Bry (An Amer. Place), July 1949: 'Abstraction, No. 11' 1915. Charcoal. Was in MOMA O'Keeffe exh. On permanent loan to the Metropolitan Museum of Art from Georgia O'Keeffe as part of the Alfred Stieglitz Coll." Abiquiú Notebooks indicates, "Note: Part of the Alfred Stieglitz Collection at Met under the title: 'Abstraction No. 11,' 1915, charcoal, 24 1/4 x 18 7/8." Whitney Archive, Abiquiú Notebooks mistakenly identify as "Drawing No. 11 Special," and Abiquiú Notebooks confuses this entry with *Special XIII*, see cat. no. 157, whose backing has label inscribed, albeit mistakenly, "Drawing No. 11 Special" (Alfred Stieglitz, An American Place, black ink). There is no known work title "Drawing No. 11 Special." Whitney Archive, Abiquiú Notebooks date 1915; O'Keeffe dates 1916 and indicates inspired by fall 1916 camping trip: "*Abstraction IX* was first made with charcoal, then it was painted many times with red, and I finally went back to the charcoal. ... I had been walking for a couple of weeks with a girl in the big woods somewhere in the North Carolina mountains. One morning before daylight, as I was combing my hair, I turned and saw her lying there—one arm thrown back, hair a dark mass against the white, the face half turned, the red mouth. It all looked warm with sleep" (*Some Memories of Drawings* [1988], unpaginated). Date confirmed on basis of Stieglitz–O'Keeffe correspondence. Pictured in 1917 New York (291) Stieglitz installation photograph, see Appendix III, figure 4. Another work in this series is known only through 1917 New York (291) Stieglitz installation photograph, see Appendix II, no. 7 and Appendix III, figure 8. (Source: Lynes, 1999)

description: Looping black lines run across the paper, encircling the head and neck of a reclining person. A small, teardrop-shaped form in the center of the face denotes the person's lips. These forms are set against the plain white background of exposed paper.
